title: Navigating the Milky Way
caption: The Milky Way over the Blanco and SMARTS–GSU telescopes, Cerro Tololo
celestial: Landscape photograph; the source does not name the site
credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/P. Horálek (Institute of Physics in Opava), M. Kosari

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The Milky Way stretches like a river of stars and dust between two telescopes at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory, an observatory of the U.S. National Science Foundation and a Program of NSF NOIRLab. On the left stands the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope, and on the right the SMARTS–GSU 1.5-meter Telescope.

Like a real river, the Milky Way is easier to navigate with landmarks, and constellations fill that role. Left of center is Sagittarius, which contains a pattern of stars known as the Teapot. The Teapot points toward the center of our galaxy, home to the supermassive black hole Sagittarius A*.

Right of center is Scorpius, a standout in the sky thanks to the bright red supergiant star Antares. Often called the heart of the scorpion, Antares can also be used to find the way to the Galactic core.

understand.summary: A night-sky photograph by Petr Horálek, part of a fulldome image. No camera or exposure details or color mapping are published.
understand.eye: No exposure details are published, so it is unclear how closely the photograph matches what an eye would see from Cerro Tololo.

explore: Petr Horálek, a NOIRLab Audiovisual Ambassador, took the photo during the NOIRLab 2022 Photo Expedition to all of NOIRLab's sites. It is part of a fulldome photo and can also be viewed as a panorama.
